Patient 2 had multiple muscle deficiencies but normal fibroblast complex I/V assembly and complex IV holocomplex; complex IV activity was low only in the mitochondrial isolate. Reduced synthesis of mtDNA-encoded subunits supports the OXPHOS defect, but does not fully explain disproportionate complex IV involvement.

evidence.snippet: The enzyme deficiency was most pronounced in cardiac muscle tissue, where there was massive proliferation of mitochondria on electron microscopy displacing contractile elements.

edges/3.description: Cardiomyocytes respond to the translation block by amplifying mtDNA and mitochondrial transcripts, a response that cannot restore protein output. evidence.snippet: These findings indicate that mitochondrial ribosomal subunit defects can generate tissue-specific manifestations, such as cardiomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: The original authors infer cardiac disease from the genetic and functional findings; this is an etiologic interpretation, not a fully reconstructed cardiac pathway.

edges/6.description: Mitoribosomal dysfunction is causally implicated in MRPL44 cardiomyopathy by patient genetics and complementation of the cell defect. The route from impaired translation to cardiac hypertrophic remodeling remains incompletely resolved.

genes/0.notes: MRPL44 (2q36.1) encodes mL44, a 39S mitoribosomal protein with an RNase III-like domain spanning residues 86–228. Patient genotypes containing p.Leu156Arg, p.Leu156Pro or p.Thr161Serfs*2 showed reduced mL44 abundance; the compound-heterozygous assays did not resolve residual protein from each individual allele. The p.Arg78Gln allele and the 2025 p.(Trp66_His69delinsCysAsn) allele lie outside that domain. The reviewed sources do not establish allele-specific protein-abundance effects for them; the 2025 delins interpretation is computational and its formal classification remains VUS. These case reports do not establish population allele frequencies or validated modifier effects.

hypotheses/0.description: A single-patient preprint proposes that nutrient-dependent mitochondrial stress contributes to perinatal hypertrophy. One homozygous p.Leu156Arg iPSC line was compared with three healthy donor lines, without an isogenic correction. The 72-hour media comparison used 2 g/L glucose versus 1 g/L glucose with oleate 100 μM and palmitate 50 μM, not glucose-free fatty-acid conditions. In glucose-rich medium, mtDNA copy number, mitochondrial area and transcripts increased despite reduced complex I protein. Lipid-enriched medium induced mitochondrial and partial ER stress, with XBP1 expression but no splicing and no FGF21 induction. Transcript-based mTOR prediction and inferred lipid utilization do not measure mTOR activity or fatty-acid oxidation flux. The proposed contribution to hypertrophic growth remains provisional and does not justify dietary treatment.

open_questions/0.rationale: In most mitochondrial transcription and translation defects, complex I (seven mtDNA-encoded subunits) is more affected than complex IV (three) simply through subunit stoichiometry. MRPL44 deficiency inverts this, as do LRPPRC and TACO1 disease. The 2021 functional study excluded the obvious explanation by showing that the newly synthesized complex IV subunits (MT-CO1, MT-CO2, MT-CO3) were reduced to approximately the same degree as complex I subunits (average 30.1% versus 34.3% of controls, not significantly different). A difference in post-synthetic stability of the assembled subunits was proposed but could not be excluded or confirmed. Resolving this matters because a complex IV-selective post-translational bottleneck would be a different therapeutic target from generic mitoribosome insufficiency.

open_questions/1.rationale: Yeast MrpL3/mL44 is the tractable genetic model for mL44 function, and mutagenesis of its conserved hydrophobic pocket does identify residues critical for assembling translationally active mitoribosomes. However, the exact human disease substitution modelled at the equivalent yeast residue (A186) had no major functional impact, and the authors concluded the two orthologs have diverged in evolution. Mouse Mrpl44 loss is a different kind of mismatch: knockout is embryonically lethal, whereas human patients carry hypomorphic alleles with residual protein and survive with tissue-restricted disease. Neither model therefore reproduces the human hypomorphic, cardiac-selective genotype-phenotype relationship, and both should be treated as tools for general mitoribosome biology rather than as MRPL44 disease models. Patient-derived iPSC cardiomyocytes are the emerging replacement, but the only published line covers a single genotype and the work remains a preprint.

evidence.snippet: we observed that mutation of the MrpL3/mL44 does not impact the translation of all mitochondrial encoded proteins equally, suggesting the mitochondrial translation system may exhibit a transcript hierarchy and prioritization.

open_questions/2.rationale: mL44 protein levels are reduced in heart, skeletal muscle, and fibroblasts alike, yet the enzymatic and clinical consequences are overwhelmingly cardiac. Candidate explanations include the higher OXPHOS flux demand and mitochondrial density of the myocardium, the postnatal switch to fatty-acid oxidation (the nutrient-dependent hypothesis), tissue-specific differences in mitoribosome assembly-factor buffering, and a possible transcript hierarchy in mitochondrial translation - the yeast work showed that MrpL3/mL44 mutation does not affect all mtDNA-encoded transcripts equally. Distinguishing a threshold effect from a genuinely cardiac-specific mechanism is required before extrapolating any therapy tested in fibroblasts to the heart.

evidence.snippet: Our findings indicate that glucose and lipids, the latter being the postnatally favored cardiac fuel, exert remarkably different consequences in MRPL44 deficient cardiomyocytes.
evidence.explanation: States the finding whose in-vivo validity and therapeutic tractability are the open question. Preprint, single patient line.

open_questions/3.rationale: The nutrient-dependent model is currently supported by a single unreviewed preprint using one patient iPSC line in short-term culture, with immature in-vitro cardiomyocyte physiology. It is mechanistically attractive because it would explain the otherwise puzzling perinatal timing of disease onset, and because it points to a stress-signalling rather than purely bioenergetic target. It must not, however, be translated into fat restriction, ketogenic diet, or any other dietary manipulation: no clinical evidence supports this, and fasting/catabolic stress is itself a recognized hazard in mitochondrial disease. Replication across genotypes, in matured or engineered heart tissue, and ideally in vivo is required.

evidence.snippet: She presented on the second day of life with Kussmaul breathing due to metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.0, base excess – 27 mEq/L), with elevated lactate 19 mmol/L (normal < 2 mmol/L) and mildly elevated ammonia 180 μM (normal < 100 μM).
evidence.explanation: Patient 2’s neonatal metabolic episode defines the acidosis, breathing and ammonia findings; the source does not resolve the intrinsic metabolic pathway.

evidence.snippet: We describe two infants who presented with cardiomyopathy from the neonatal period, failure to thrive, hypoglycemia and in one infant lactic acidosis.
evidence.explanation: The two-infant clinical summary establishes the recurring metabolic/growth presentation, not its separate tissue mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: Chromosomal microarray revealed a deletion of 16q23.3
evidence.explanation: The first infant’s additional chromosome deletion limits exclusive attribution of every isolated finding to MRPL44.

open_questions/4.rationale: The infant report establishes neonatal acidosis, hypoglycemia and feeding difficulty, with transient hyperammonemia in Patient 2 and hypothermia in Patient 1. A qualified OXPHOS-to-lactic-acidosis route is represented using established pyruvate/redox physiology and the MRPL44 clinical measurements; missing tissue-level reconstruction does not negate that relation. The precise tissue contribution and possible cardiac/illness amplification remain unresolved. Intrinsic hypoglycemia, hypothermia, hyperammonemia and feeding difficulty are less causally localized by these sources. Hypoglycemia preceded cardiac shock; the shock link concerns its acute exacerbation only. Feeding insufficiency has a supported nutritional route to poor growth. Patient 1 also carried a 16q23.3 deletion. No blanket ATP-depletion fanout is asserted.

evidence.snippet: A rare mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation disorder with complex I and IV deficiency characterized by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hepatic steatosis with elevated liver transaminases, exercise intolerance and muscle weakness.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's expert clinical definition includes hepatic steatosis with elevated liver transaminases as a characteristic feature.

evidence.snippet: However, we observed several additional clinical signs and symptoms including pigmentary retinopathy, hemiplegic migraine, Leigh-like lesions on brain MRI, renal insufficiency, and hepatopathy.
evidence.explanation: Reports renal insufficiency among the additional features of the two patients in this series. No frequency band is assigned: the source enumerates features without per-patient attribution or any count, so any band would be unsupported.

open_questions/5.rationale: Chronic renal insufficiency and hepatopathy occur in the multisystem literature; the Orphanet definition specifies steatosis and elevated transaminases. These sources do not establish a renal cell compartment or demonstrate a liver-specific lipid/ATP pathway. The infant’s renal dysfunction and hepatic failure during shock support separately qualified secondary circulatory routes, which must not be transferred to the chronic organ findings. Cardiac iPSC lipid droplets are not evidence for a hepatocyte steatosis mechanism.

evidence.snippet: At nine months of age during a respiratory syncytial viral infection, she was admitted for hypoxia and had respiratory failure for ten days after which she recovered back to baseline.
evidence.explanation: The acute respiratory failure was infection-associated. It does not establish primary chronic pulmonary involvement from MRPL44.

open_questions/6.rationale: The source reports respiratory failure during RSV infection with recovery to baseline, followed by a separate cardiac shock admission. A direct MRPL44 pulmonary or respiratory-muscle mechanism was not established. The source-supported acidosis-to-Kussmaul route and qualified shock-to-hypoxia route explain those particular components without explaining the infection itself.

evidence.snippet: confirms that MRLP44 mutations cause a mitochondrial translation defect that may present as a multisystem disorder with neurological involvement.
evidence.explanation: The authors’ causal interpretation supports the broad syndrome attribution while leaving tissue intermediates unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Our findings expand the clinical spectrum associated with MRPL44 mutations and indicate that MRPL44-associated mitochondrial dysfunction can also manifest as a progressive multisystem disease with central nervous system involvement.
evidence.explanation: The independent clinical report supports a multisystem mitochondrial interpretation, without identifying specific downstream cellular mediators.

open_questions/7.rationale: The clinical reports explicitly attribute the multisystem disorder to MRPL44-related mitochondrial dysfunction, and Horga links the adult phenotype to a demonstrable translation defect. Those qualified causal attributions are represented even though intervening tissue mechanisms are unknown. No measured chronic ATP deficit is claimed in kidney, liver, retina or brain, and MRI distribution alone is not taken as proof that a particular lesion causes ataxia, spasticity or migraine. Case-specific modifiers remain possible, particularly in the chromosome 2 isodisomy case.

evidence.snippet: The fourth patient from age 14 years on developed cardiomyopathy, hemiplegic migraines, learning difficulties, myopathy, tapetoretinal dystrophy, and Leigh-like lesions in thalami, basal ganglia and cerebellum on brain MRI
evidence.explanation: The report names learning difficulties without identifying a specific academic-skill deficit or excluding general cognitive impairment in that individual; the broader cognitive term avoids an unsupported specific-learning-disability claim.

evidence.snippet: However, we observed several additional clinical signs and symptoms including pigmentary retinopathy, hemiplegic migraine, Leigh-like lesions on brain MRI, renal insufficiency, and hepatopathy.
evidence.explanation: The two-case report includes hemiplegic migraine. The generic Migraine binding retains the motor subtype in the name: the current HPO Migraine with aura definition explicitly excludes motor weakness, and no dedicated hemiplegic-migraine HP term was retrieved. No frequency is inferred.

open_questions/8.rationale: The 2013, 2015 and adult-2021 primary abstracts were read, and detailed case observations were checked against the full 2021 infant paper, which explicitly summarizes the earlier cases. Accessible DOI fetches did not provide full text of the 2015 or adult-2021 reports; no inaccessible table was treated as read. GeneReviews PMID20301403 is an umbrella overview, not an MRPL44-specific chapter or phenotype baseline. Cognitive impairment replaces a specific-learning-disability term because the source does not identify a particular academic skill deficit. Migraine is retained as the broader binding because the current Migraine with aura HPO definition excludes motor weakness and a dedicated hemiplegic term was not retrieved. Regional Leigh-like MRI findings remain in imaging_findings; central cores and hypercontracted fibers are preserved as biopsy observations, not invented causal nodes.

evidence.snippet: We report on eight new cases of this condition, two of whom were shown to have heterozygous missense mutations in the C-terminal zinc finger domains of WT1: Arg366Cys and Arg394Trp.
evidence.explanation: This Meacham syndrome case series directly links the disorder to heterozygous WT1 zinc finger missense variants.

evidence.snippet: WT1 is a versatile gene that controls transitions between the mesenchymal and epithelial state of cells in a tissue-context dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: This WT1 disease review supports the mechanistic inference that WT1 variants in Meacham syndrome disrupt developmental epithelial-mesenchymal state control.

steps/1.description: Meacham syndrome is caused by heterozygous missense variants in the C-terminal zinc finger DNA-binding domains of WT1. These variants disrupt WT1-dependent transcriptional control of embryonic mesenchymal-epithelial state transitions and developmental patterning across the diaphragm, heart, and gonads.

evidence.snippet: These data represent clinical and molecular evidence that the WT1 gene plays a central role in normal development of the diaphragm and the proepicardially derived tissues.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports the core developmental mechanism linking WT1 dysfunction to combined diaphragmatic and cardiac malformations.

evidence.snippet: Identification of WT1 expression in the region of coelomic mesothelium which will form the proepicardium and diaphragm provides a plausible unifying patterning defect in these cases.
evidence.explanation: This supports a coelomic mesothelial developmental defect as the unifying anatomic mechanism in Meacham syndrome.

steps/2.description: WT1 dysfunction in coelomic mesothelium impairs diaphragm development and development of proepicardially derived cardiac tissues, providing a unifying developmental explanation for the combined diaphragmatic and complex cardiac malformations in Meacham syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The retention of Müllerian structures and undervirilization of male genitalia in these cases could be the result of failure in production of adequate amounts of testosterone and Müllerian inhibitory factor at appropriate times in gestation.
evidence.explanation: The original Meacham report directly connects retained Müllerian structures and undervirilization to disrupted fetal testicular endocrine signaling, supporting this organ-specific downstream mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Additional common findings can include disorders of testicular development (with or without abnormalities of the external genitalia and/or müllerian structures) and Wilms tumor.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews places disorders of testicular development and Müllerian structure abnormalities within the WT1 disorder spectrum.

steps/3.description: WT1-related gonadal developmental disruption in 46,XY embryos can impair fetal testicular differentiation, androgen production, and Müllerian inhibitory factor activity, producing undervirilization and persistent Müllerian structures.

evidence.snippet: Identification of WT1 expression in the region of coelomic mesothelium which will form the proepicardium and diaphragm provides a plausible unifying patterning defect in these cases.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports the causal link from WT1 dysfunction to a shared coelomic mesothelial developmental defect.

edges/1.description: WT1 dysfunction perturbs diaphragm and proepicardial tissue development

evidence.snippet: The retention of Müllerian structures and undervirilization of male genitalia in these cases could be the result of failure in production of adequate amounts of testosterone and Müllerian inhibitory factor at appropriate times in gestation.
evidence.explanation: The original Meacham case report provides a phenotype-linked mechanism for retained Müllerian structures and undervirilization.

edges/2.description: WT1-related gonadal developmental disruption can impair fetal testicular differentiation and the testosterone/Müllerian-inhibitory-factor program needed for virilization and Müllerian regression.

evidence.snippet: We report on eight new cases of this condition, two of whom were shown to have heterozygous missense mutations in the C-terminal zinc finger domains of WT1: Arg366Cys and Arg394Trp.
evidence.explanation: This is direct human genetic evidence that heterozygous WT1 missense variants cause Meacham syndrome in at least a subset of cases.

evidence.snippet: Historically, specific mutations in WT1 gene have been associated with distinct syndromes based on phenotypic characteristics, including Denys-Drash syndrome (DDS), Frasier syndrome (FS), Meacham syndrome, and WAGR syndrome.
evidence.explanation: This review supports placing Meacham syndrome within the broader WT1-related disorder spectrum.

genes/0.notes: Meacham syndrome is caused by heterozygous WT1 missense variants, especially in the C-terminal zinc finger DNA-binding domains. WT1-associated Meacham syndrome is now considered part of the broader WT1-related disorder continuum.

evidence.snippet: Diaphragmatic hernia repair prior to the start of peritoneal dialysis.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly names diaphragmatic hernia repair as a management step in WT1 disorder, supporting its relevance for Meacham syndrome patients with congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

treatments/0.description: Surgical repair of congenital diaphragmatic defects is a core management intervention for affected individuals with Meacham syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Prevent whenever possible gonadoblastoma by prophylactic gonadectomy in those with a disorder of testicular development.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management guidance for WT1 disorder supports prophylactic gonadectomy as a relevant treatment consideration for Meacham syndrome patients with WT1-related testicular developmental abnormalities.

treatments/1.description: In WT1-related disorders with testicular developmental abnormalities, prophylactic gonadectomy is used to reduce gonadoblastoma risk and may be relevant to Meacham syndrome patients with marked gonadal dysgenesis.

evidence.snippet: Disorders of testicular development and 46,XX gonadal dysgenesis: management is often by a multidisciplinary team (clinical geneticist, endocrinologist, urologist, and psychologist).
evidence.explanation: This supports multidisciplinary specialty care as a treatment-relevant management approach for WT1-related sex development disorders including Meacham syndrome.

treatments/2.description: Management of WT1-related disorders with gonadal and genital anomalies requires coordinated care involving genetics, endocrinology, urology, and psychological support.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: Monitor for first appearance of the following: proteinuria every six months until age ten years, yearly thereafter; Wilms tumor every three months until age seven years; early gonadal insufficiency yearly after puberty.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews gives the WT1 disorder surveillance interval for Wilms tumor, supporting this survivor-specific management recommendation.

treatments/3.description: WT1-confirmed Meacham survivors should receive WT1-disorder tumor surveillance, including Wilms tumor screening every three months until age seven years, while recognizing that Wilms tumor is not a defining feature of the classic early-lethal Meacham presentation.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: Monitor for first appearance of the following: proteinuria every six months until age ten years, yearly thereafter; Wilms tumor every three months until age seven years; early gonadal insufficiency yearly after puberty.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports proteinuria surveillance for individuals with WT1 disorder.

treatments/4.description: WT1-confirmed survivors should be monitored for renal disease with proteinuria surveillance every six months until age ten years and yearly thereafter, because nephropathy belongs to the WT1 disorder spectrum even when it is not a core Meacham-defining feature.

evidence.snippet: In adulthood, most individuals are affected by early gonadal insufficiency of variable severity with potential impact on puberty and fertility.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports monitoring and management of gonadal insufficiency and puberty/fertility effects in WT1 disorder.

treatments/5.description: Endocrinology follow-up should address early gonadal insufficiency after puberty and hormone replacement when clinically indicated after gonadectomy or severe gonadal dysgenesis.

evidence.snippet: Both infants had complex cyanotic congenital heart defects, hypoplastic right lungs, anomalous pulmonary venous return, and abnormalities of the diaphragm.
evidence.explanation: The severity of the reported congenital heart defects supports explicit cardiology management in affected infants.

treatments/6.description: Affected infants with structural heart disease require cardiology-led assessment, supportive management, and congenital cardiac intervention when anatomically appropriate.

evidence.snippet: WT1 disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Most individuals diagnosed with WT1 disorder have the disorder as the result of an apparent de novo WT1 pathogenic variant;
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports autosomal dominant inheritance and the frequent de novo origin relevant to recurrence-risk counseling.

treatments/7.description: Genetic counseling should cover autosomal dominant WT1 disorder inheritance, the frequent de novo origin of pathogenic variants, recurrence risk when a parent carries the familial variant, parental gonadal mosaicism, and prenatal or preimplantation testing once the familial WT1 variant is known.

evidence.snippet: We used whole exome and whole genome sequencing to identify recessively inherited variants in NDUFC2 (NM_004549.6; c.346_*7del, p.(His116_Arg119delins21) in one family with two affected siblings and a different recessively inherited variant (c.173A>T, p.(His58Leu)) in an affected individual from an unrelated family.
evidence.explanation: Both alleles with full nomenclature, and how each family was ascertained.

evidence.snippet: Review of the gnomAD variant database revealed no homozygous loss-of-function variants within NDUFC2
evidence.explanation: The population-database argument that biallelic NDUFC2 loss is not tolerated, which is part of what makes the variants credible as causal.

evidence.snippet: NDUFC2 | HGNC:7706 | mitochondrial disease | MONDO:0044970 | AR | Moderate | SOP9
evidence.explanation: Independent expert-panel classification of the gene-disease relationship, its inheritance mode and its strength. Graded OTHER because a curation assertion is an expert judgement rather than a study.

steps/1.description: Two damaged copies of NDUFC2. Two alleles are known and each is homozygous in one family. The Saudi siblings carry c.346_*7del, a 22-nucleotide deletion that removes the stop codon and replaces the last four residues with a 21-residue extension, p.(His116_Arg119delins21). The Moroccan boy carries c.173A>T, p.(His58Leu), at a histidine conserved across species, with every in silico predictor calling it damaging. Neither allele class is present homozygously in population databases: gnomAD contains no homozygous loss-of-function NDUFC2 variant at all.

evidence.snippet: NDUFC2 is a membrane protein assigned to the ND2 module within the proton pumping modules
evidence.explanation: Where the protein sits in the enzyme, which sets what its loss can disrupt.

evidence.snippet: The protein locates to the intermembrane space and has contact with 12 other subunits
evidence.explanation: The connectivity that makes NDUFC2 a hub. It is the single fact that best explains why losing one small subunit takes two whole modules with it.

evidence.snippet: Complexome profiling confirmed a loss of NDUFC2 and defective complex I assembly
evidence.explanation: The measurement of the protein's absence in patient mitochondria.

steps/2.description: NDUFC2 is a membrane protein of the proton-pumping arm, assigned to the ND2 module, facing the intermembrane space, and in contact with twelve other subunits - NDUFA8 in the ND1 module, five subunits of its own ND2 module, and five of the ND4 module. That is an unusual amount of connectivity for a small accessory subunit and is the structural reason a defect in it is an assembly defect rather than a catalytic one. Complexome profiling of patient fibroblasts confirms the loss of NDUFC2 itself.

evidence.snippet: Complexome profiling of both subjects is consistent with this model, where loss of NDUFC2 causes concurrent loss of its associating subunits
evidence.explanation: The core assembly result, in both patients.

evidence.snippet: It is possible that NDUFC2 may represent a scaffold for ND1 module formation; the absence of stable ND1 and ND2 modules indicates that these proximal P-modules do not preassemble independently.
evidence.explanation: The mechanistic reading, with the hedge the authors put on the scaffold hypothesis and the firmer conclusion about proximal module interdependence that follows from the same data.

evidence.snippet: Neither the ND5 module nor the N module intermediates were identified in the complexome data from the NDUFC2 subjects.
evidence.explanation: The negative that bounds the defect: the downstream modules are not merely delayed, they are not detectable as intermediates at all.

steps/3.description: Losing NDUFC2 takes its neighbours with it. Complexome profiling of both index patients shows concurrent loss of the subunits NDUFC2 associates with, in the ND1 and ND2 modules. The negative results are as informative as the positive ones: neither an ND5 nor an N module intermediate was found at all, while the distal ND4 module was still detected - so the distal membrane module assembles independently while the two proximal ones do not. The authors read this as NDUFC2 possibly acting as a scaffold for ND1 module formation.

evidence.snippet: Our data support successful formation of the Q module with subsequent assembly stalling due to failed incorporation of the ND1 subunit into the inner mitochondrial membrane.
evidence.explanation: Where the assembly line stops, and the step at which it stops - which is what distinguishes a stall from a general failure to assemble.

evidence.snippet: demonstrated undetectable levels of fully assembled complex I in Subject 1 and greatly decreased assembled complex I in Subject 3 compared to controls; all other OXPHOS complexes were unaffected
evidence.explanation: The endpoint of the stall in each patient, and the observation that makes the deficiency isolated rather than combined.

steps/4.description: Assembly does not fail from the start - it gets part-way and stops. The Q module forms successfully, and the process then halts because the ND1 subunit is not incorporated into the inner membrane, leaving aberrant intermediates rather than holoenzyme. In one patient's fibroblasts no fully assembled complex I was detectable at all; in the other it was greatly decreased. All other oxidative phosphorylation complexes were unaffected, which is what makes the deficiency isolated.

evidence.snippet: Assessment of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme activities revealed a severe and isolated complex I deficiency in the fibroblasts from Subject 1 (16% residual activity compared to controls)
evidence.explanation: The quantified deficiency in the first index patient.

evidence.snippet: Identification of an isolated complex I defect in Subject 3's muscle biopsy prompted genetic studies which identified a homozygous c.173A>T, p.(His58Leu) NDUFC2 variant
evidence.explanation: The deficiency in patient muscle rather than in culture, and the fact that it was the finding that triggered the genetic diagnosis in that family.

steps/5.description: The measured biochemical endpoint and the phenotype the entity is named for. Residual complex I activity was 16 percent of control in one patient's fibroblasts and 19 percent in the other's, with 48 percent in that patient's muscle - so the deficiency is severe but graded, and tissue-dependent. Lentiviral expression of wild-type NDUFC2 raised both the steady-state subunit levels and the amount of assembled complex I, without reaching control levels in either line.

evidence.snippet: BN-PAGE analysis of digitonin-solubilised fibroblast mitochondrial preparations demonstrated a dramatic deficiency of complex I-containing supercomplexes
evidence.explanation: The measurement, and the solubilisation condition that makes supercomplexes visible.

steps/6.description: Complex I does not work alone: it associates with complexes III and IV into supercomplexes, and those are lost too. Blue native electrophoresis of digitonin-solubilised patient mitochondria shows a dramatic deficiency of the complex I-containing supercomplexes. This is a consequence of having no holoenzyme to incorporate rather than a separate lesion, but it is worth recording as its own node because it is what the respiratory measurements are made against.

evidence.snippet: High-resolution respirometry revealed both subjects' cell lines exhibited severely decreased rates of oxygen consumption
evidence.explanation: The functional readout in intact cells, in both patients, which is what turns an enzymology number into a statement about cellular energy supply.

steps/7.description: The cellular consequence, measured directly. High-resolution respirometry of intact cells shows severely decreased oxygen consumption in both patients' fibroblast lines. A cell that cannot oxidise NADH through complex I cannot maintain normal electron flux into the rest of the chain, and the shortfall shows as reduced respiration rather than as a compensated steady state.

evidence.snippet: we describe three subjects from independent consanguineous families whose clinical presentations were consistent with a diagnosis of Leigh syndrome and who exhibited radiological lesions of the basal ganglia, thalami and substantia nigra
evidence.explanation: The distribution of the lesion across all three patients, in the authors' own summary.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI revealed bilateral abnormal high T2 signal intensity within the thalami
evidence.explanation: The imaging finding in the third patient, at five months of age.

steps/8.description: The tissue lesion that defines Leigh syndrome, and it is present in all three children. Imaging showed bilateral symmetrical high T2 signal in the thalami, substantia nigra and medulla in the first patient, in the basal ganglia and lentiform nuclei in her brother, and in the thalami, basal ganglia and brainstem in the third. The first patient also had corticospinal-tract signal change with white matter volume loss and periventricular leukomalacia; the second had a Dandy-Walker malformation with partial corpus callosum agenesis, which is a malformation rather than a degenerative lesion and is recorded as its own phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Routine blood investigations including plasma amino acid levels were reported normal, but serum lactate and pyruvate levels were elevated
evidence.explanation: Both metabolites raised together in the third patient, which places the block upstream of pyruvate oxidation.

evidence.snippet: Plasma amino acid analysis detected elevated alanine (724 μmol/l, normal range 143–439 μmol/l) and elevated proline (366 μmol/l, normal range 52–298 μmol/l).
evidence.explanation: The amino-acid correlate of chronic pyruvate accumulation in the first patient, with the reference intervals the laboratory used.

steps/9.description: Every reported patient had elevated serum lactate - 3.6 to 7.6 mmol per litre in the first, 4.0 to 10.0 in her brother and above 20 during an intercurrent illness, and 3.2 in the third, whose pyruvate was raised as well. Two of the three also had elevated plasma alanine, the transamination product of accumulated pyruvate, and one had raised proline and increased urinary fumarate.

evidence.snippet: Assessment of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme activities revealed a severe and isolated complex I deficiency in the fibroblasts from Subject 1 (16% residual activity compared to controls)
evidence.explanation: The quantified deficiency, with the residual figure.

evidence.snippet: Similar investigations for Subject 2 were not possible due to a lack of available samples for analysis
evidence.explanation: Why the assay denominator is two of three, recorded rather than left as an implied gap.

steps/10.description: The defining biochemical finding: 16 percent residual activity in one patient's fibroblasts, 19 percent in the other's and 48 percent in that patient's muscle, with all other respiratory chain complexes normal.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe three affected children from two unrelated families who presented with Leigh syndrome due to homozygous variants (c.346_*7del and c.173A>T p.His58Leu) in NDUFC2, encoding a complex I subunit.
evidence.explanation: The clinical diagnosis in all three, stated with the genotypes.

evidence.snippet: The NDUFC2 gene was first reported in relation to autosomal recessive Leigh syndrome spectrum in 2020
evidence.explanation: The expert panel's framing of the same relationship. Graded OTHER because a curation narrative is an expert synthesis rather than a study.

steps/11.description: All three children were diagnosed with Leigh syndrome, and the entity entered the literature under that name. It is the presentation for which ClinGen first curated the gene.

evidence.snippet: Following birth, he was noted to have persistently elevated serum lactate (4.0–10.0 mmol/l; normal range 0.7–2.2 mmol/l).
evidence.explanation: The lactate elevation in the second patient, with the laboratory's reference interval.

evidence.snippet: Serum lactate ranged from 3.6 to 7.6 mmol/l (normal range 0.7–2.2 mmol/l), whilst ammonia, blood glucose and thyroid function were unremarkable.
evidence.explanation: The same finding in the first patient, together with the negatives that make it a specific rather than a general metabolic derangement.

steps/12.description: Raised serum lactate in all three children, from 3.2 to 10.0 mmol per litre at baseline against a normal range topping out at about 2.2, and above 20 in one child during an intercurrent illness.

evidence.snippet: He exhibited global developmental delay and poor growth with his weight and length remaining below the 3rd centile.
evidence.explanation: The delay in the second patient, with the growth failure alongside it.

evidence.snippet: Vomiting, failure to thrive, psychomotor delay and poor eye contact were reported from the first months of life.
evidence.explanation: The onset in the third patient, which is the earliest documented in the series.

steps/13.description: Developmental impairment in all three: unable to walk at two years and unable to stand unsupported or speak at six in the first patient, global delay with poor growth in her brother, and psychomotor delay from the first months of life in the third.

evidence.snippet: clinical examination revealed facial dysmorphic features, spasticity and brisk deep tendon reflexes
evidence.explanation: The upper motor neuron signs in the first patient at six years.

evidence.snippet: His clinical course was dominated by progressive spasticity, muscle atrophy, development of a left hydronephrosis and a persistent lactic acidosis.
evidence.explanation: The same feature in the second patient, and its place in his overall course.

steps/14.description: Spasticity with brisk reflexes in the first patient at six years, and progressive spasticity with muscle atrophy dominating the second patient's course. The third had truncal hypotonia with limb hypertonia instead, which is a different tone pattern and is described rather than counted here.

evidence.snippet: With this intercurrent illness, he developed seizures, regressed and lost all of his previously acquired developmental skills.
evidence.explanation: The second patient's seizures and the regression that came with the same illness.

evidence.snippet: She did not develop seizures and had no cardiac, renal or hepatic abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: The negative in the first patient, which is why this is FREQUENT rather than OBLIGATE and why the cardiac finding below is not general to the disease.

steps/15.description: Seizures in two of the three children, and in both cases provoked rather than spontaneous at onset: the second developed them during a severe respiratory infection at nineteen months, and the third had intermittent clonic seizures of the upper limbs under anaesthesia. The first child explicitly did not develop seizures.

evidence.snippet: With this intercurrent illness, he developed seizures, regressed and lost all of his previously acquired developmental skills.
evidence.explanation: The regression, and the trigger it followed.

steps/16.description: Loss of all previously acquired developmental skills in the second patient, triggered by a severe respiratory infection at nineteen months. Regression provoked by intercurrent illness is the characteristic tempo of Leigh syndrome and is what distinguishes it from a static encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: A hearing assessment was unremarkable, but an ophthalmological examination revealed bilateral optic disc pallor.
evidence.explanation: The optic finding, with the negative hearing assessment in the same sentence that bounds the sensory involvement.

steps/17.description: Bilateral optic disc pallor in the first patient at six years, on an ophthalmological examination that followed an unremarkable hearing assessment. The third patient had poor eye contact and severe central conduction abnormalities on visual evoked potentials, which is a different finding and is described rather than counted here.

evidence.snippet: Plasma amino acid analysis detected elevated alanine (724 μmol/l, normal range 143–439 μmol/l) and elevated proline (366 μmol/l, normal range 52–298 μmol/l).
evidence.explanation: The measurement with its reference interval.

evidence.snippet: Routine blood investigations including plasma amino acid levels were reported normal, but serum lactate and pyruvate levels were elevated
evidence.explanation: The contrary finding in the third patient, recorded so that a normal amino-acid profile is not read as excluding the diagnosis.

steps/18.description: Elevated plasma alanine in the first patient, the expected transamination product of accumulated pyruvate and a standard secondary marker of a respiratory chain block. Notably it was normal in the third patient, whose lactate and pyruvate were both raised.

edges/10.description: Pyruvate that cannot be oxidised is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+, which is the standard route from a complex I block to a lactic acidosis.

evidence.snippet: Our study documents the first cases of mitochondrial disease caused by variants in the NDUFC2 gene.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease relationship as established, and its novelty at the time.

evidence.snippet: our results clearly demonstrate that lentiviral expression of wild-type NDUFC2 ameliorates the phenotype, leading not only to increased steady-state levels of complex I subunits, but of their incorporation into the holoenzyme
evidence.explanation: The complementation result that converts an association into a causal claim, and the two levels at which the rescue was measured.

evidence.snippet: In summary, there is moderate evidence to support the relationship between NDUFC2 and primary mitochondrial disease.
evidence.explanation: The independent strength-of-evidence judgement, which is Moderate rather than Definitive and is a fair reflection of a two-family series with strong functional data.

genes/0.notes:
NDUFC2 encodes NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase subunit C2, a small membrane subunit of the proton-pumping arm of complex I. Its structural position, in the ND2 module facing the intermembrane space with contacts to twelve other subunits across three modules, is the whole mechanism of this disease and is curated as its own pathophysiology node.
Two traps for anyone extending this entry from the gene rather than from the disease, and both are easy to fall into because they dominate a naive literature search.
First, NDUFC2 carries a large cardiovascular and complex-trait association literature - polymorphic variants and cardiac hypertrophy in human hypertension, autophagy and hypertension-related stroke, glucose metabolism in recombinant inbred mice, Mendelian randomisation studies of hyperuricaemia, psychiatric multi-omics, melanoma. None of it concerns this disease, and none of it is cited here. The gene is common-variant interesting and rare-variant interesting for entirely different reasons.
Second, there is a separate HGNC entity, NDUFC2-KCTD14 (HGNC:42956), a readthrough transcript, and several association signals in this genomic region are reported against the readthrough rather than against NDUFC2 itself. The binding in this entry is hgnc:7706, the protein-coding gene, and a search that does not separate the two will conflate them.

evidence.snippet: Brain CT scan detected acute hydrocephalus with significant dilatation of the third and lateral ventricles. He underwent urgent ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion.
evidence.explanation: The intervention and the indication for it, in the one patient who required it.

treatments/0.description: The second patient developed acute hydrocephalus at five months, on a background of an antenatally detected Dandy-Walker malformation, and had an urgent ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted. This is decompression of a structural complication, not treatment of the complex I defect, and it is the only surgical intervention reported in the series.

evidence.snippet: Recurrent chest infections and pulmonary aspirations suggested an unsafe swallow, and he was placed on nasogastric tube feeding.
evidence.explanation: The feeding intervention and the clinical problem that prompted it.

treatments/1.description: The same patient developed recurrent chest infections and pulmonary aspiration, which were taken to indicate an unsafe swallow, and was placed on nasogastric tube feeding. Securing enteral nutrition and reducing aspiration risk is standard supportive management of a progressive Leigh syndrome course, and it is the only feeding intervention recorded in this series.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical investigations into the functional consequences of the identified NDUFC2 variants showed similar findings for both Subjects 1 and 3, despite one individual harbouring a homozygous missense variant involving a highly conserved residue and the other harbouring a homozygous loss-of-function variant.
evidence.explanation: The observation itself, with the authors' own framing of it as a contrast worth remarking on.

evidence.snippet: The loss of the NDUFC2-containing ND2 module in Subject 3 asserts that the conserved His58 residue plays an important role in its assembly or stability.
evidence.explanation: The authors' explanation, and the strength of claim they attach to it. It is an assertion from a module-level observation rather than a measurement of the protein.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, there was no detectable NDUFC2 protein in Subject 1, whilst a scant amount was detectable in Subject 3 (Fig 4A, grey horizontal row); this correlated with the degree of complex I intermediates and supercomplexes detectable in each subject complexome.
evidence.explanation: The direct measurement of residual NDUFC2 abundance in both patient lines. It shows the missense subject retains a little protein where the stop-loss subject retains none, so the shared assembly phenotype is not a shared protein-level phenotype.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The two families carry very different alleles and the biochemistry does not distinguish them, which the paper states plainly. One patient is homozygous for c.346_*7del, which removes the stop codon and replaces the last four residues with a 21-residue extension. The other is homozygous for p.(His58Leu), one substitution at a conserved histidine. Residual complex I activity was 16 and 19 percent respectively, oxygen consumption was severely reduced in both, and both showed the same module-level assembly failure.
The authors' reading is that His58 matters for the assembly or stability of the ND2 module itself, so losing it is functionally equivalent to losing the subunit. That is consistent with everything measured, and it is not the only possibility: the stop-loss extension might be tolerated better than a frank truncation would be, which would raise the missense allele to meet a less severe null rather than lowering the null to meet a severe missense. Residual NDUFC2 protein has in fact been measured, and it does not separate the two accounts as cleanly as it might have. The complexome profile resolves NDUFC2 abundance directly: none is detectable in the stop-loss patient, while a scant amount is detectable in the missense patient. So the two alleles are not identical at the protein level even though the assembly phenotype converges, and the missense subject retains a little protein that is nonetheless failing to sustain the ND2 module.
It matters beyond this gene because it bears on how a missense variant in a small interface subunit should be interpreted when it is found in a new patient. If a single conserved interface residue routinely costs a whole module, then in silico conservation scores are doing more work in these genes than they usually are.
What remains open is therefore not whether the missense protein is present - it is whether that scant His58Leu protein is assembly-incompetent at the ND2 interface or merely unstable and present below the level needed to nucleate the module. Those two predict the same abundance and different incorporation behaviour.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, the NDUFC2 phenotype has been lumped into one disease entity according to the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework.
evidence.explanation: The expert panel stating its own lumping decision explicitly, which is the clearest available statement of the alternative framing.

evidence.snippet: The relationship between NDUFC2 and Leigh syndrome spectrum was evaluated using the ClinGen Clinical Validity Framework as of November 23, 2020.
evidence.explanation: The earlier framing, against the clinical syndrome rather than the gene-defined entity.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Both framings are in current use by authorities that are not disagreeing about any fact.
MONDO and OMIM file the entity in the nuclear complex I deficiency series as type 36, which is the name this entry carries. ClinGen's Mitochondrial Diseases expert panel curated NDUFC2 first against Leigh syndrome spectrum in 2020, then re-curated it in 2023 against primary mitochondrial disease, applying its lumping and splitting framework to fold the Leigh cases into a single gene-defined entity. The three published patients were all diagnosed with Leigh syndrome.
So there are three names for one set of three children, and each is defensible: a biochemical classification, a clinical syndrome, and a gene-defined entity. This entry uses the MONDO name because that is what the knowledge base keys on, curates Leigh syndrome as an OBLIGATE phenotype because it is what all three patients had, and cites the ClinGen assertions for both of that panel's framings.
Where the difference could matter is in retrieval rather than in biology. A clinician searching Leigh syndrome genes and a curator searching the MC1DN series should both find this entity, and a knowledge base that recorded only one framing would fail one of them. It also matters for how the disorder's boundaries will be drawn if a patient is reported who has NDUFC2 variants without Leigh syndrome - on the MONDO framing that patient still has MC1DN36, on the ClinGen framing they still have NDUFC2-related mitochondrial disease, and only the clinical framing would exclude them.
Worth noting for the structural record: MONDO:0030902 has exactly one superclass, MONDO:0100223 mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type, and is not placed under Leigh syndrome, so the ontology does not itself hold both framings.

evidence.snippet: Confirmation of these variants as causative enables prenatal testing of a subsequent pregnancies in these families, demonstrating the clinical importance of providing a genetic diagnosis in mitochondrial disease cases
evidence.explanation: The one clinical consequence the authors claim for the diagnosis, which is reproductive rather than therapeutic.

open_questions/2.rationale:
No. Nothing disease-modifying exists for NDUFC2 deficiency, no treatment response is reported for any of the three patients, and no trial is registered for the gene or the disorder.
What the treatments block does hold is the two supportive interventions the paper actually records, each in the same single patient: a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for acute hydrocephalus, and nasogastric tube feeding for an unsafe swallow. Both are directed at complications rather than at the complex I defect, neither is reported with an outcome, and the child died at three years. They are curated because they are documented facts about these patients, not because they constitute a management strategy. Intensive care during his respiratory crisis is described in the course rather than curated as a treatment, because the paper records it as a level of care rather than as an intervention with an indication.
The lentiviral complementation is not a treatment. It is the experiment that established causality, it is curated under experimental_models with its limitations attached, and the authors present it as support for pathogenicity rather than as a therapeutic proposal. Reading it as gene therapy in prospect would be an inference the source does not make.
Generic supportive management of Leigh syndrome, and the management recommendations in the GeneReviews Leigh syndrome spectrum chapter, are ready-made content that would look right here and are deliberately not imported. Doing so would assert of three NDUFC2 patients an experience recorded only of other people with other genotypes.
The one thing the diagnosis demonstrably changed for these families is recorded in the diagnosis block rather than here: it enabled prenatal testing in subsequent pregnancies, which the authors give as the concrete clinical value of the molecular result.

evidence.snippet: The turnover of HA requires endoglycosidic breakdown by lysosomal hyaluronidase, and a congenital deficiency of hyaluronidase has been thought to be incompatible with life.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that lysosomal hyaluronidase is required for hyaluronan turnover; its congenital deficiency is the proximal defect in MPS IX.

evidence.snippet: These genes, HYAL1 and HYAL2, encode two distinct lysosomal hyaluronidases with different substrate specificities.
evidence.explanation: Identifies HYAL1 as encoding a lysosomal hyaluronidase, the enzyme deficient in MPS IX.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in HYAL1 cause deficiency of lysosomal hyaluronidase 1, the endoglycosidase that degrades hyaluronan. Loss of this activity blocks the endoglycosidic breakdown of hyaluronan that is required for its lysosomal turnover.

evidence.snippet: Hyaluronan (HA), a large glycosaminoglycan abundant in the extracellular matrix, is important in cell migration during embryonic development, cellular proliferation, and differentiation and has a structural role in connective tissues.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the stored substrate as hyaluronan, a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix and connective tissue, distinguishing MPS IX from the sulfated-GAG mucopolysaccharidoses.

evidence.snippet: These data provide an explanation for the unexpectedly mild phenotype in mucopolysaccharidosis IX and predict the existence of other hyaluronidase deficiency disorders.
evidence.explanation: The restricted tissue impact of hyaluronan storage accounts for the unexpectedly mild MPS IX phenotype, consistent with the hub not engaging the sulfated-GAG tissue arms of the module.

steps/2.description: Undegraded hyaluronan accumulates within lysosomes. This is the GAG-accumulation hub of the mps_gag_storage module, but unlike the sulfated GAGs, hyaluronan does not engage the heparan-sulfate neuronopathic, dermatan-sulfate somatic, or keratan-sulfate skeletal arms. Hyaluronan is instead enriched in synovial fluid, cartilage, and skin, directing the downstream pathology toward the joints rather than toward the central nervous system, viscera, cornea, or generalized skeleton. This tissue distribution underlies the unexpectedly mild, joint-centred phenotype of MPS IX.

evidence.snippet: This patient had a surprisingly mild clinical phenotype, including notable periarticular soft tissue masses, mild short stature, an absence of neurological or visceral involvement, and histological and ultrastructural evidence of a lysosomal storage disease.
evidence.explanation: Defines the core MPS IX phenotype cluster: periarticular soft-tissue masses and mild short stature, with absent neurological/visceral disease.

evidence.snippet: The first reported patient had mild short stature and periarticular soft tissue masses; the other reported patients are clinically indistinguishable from juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the joint-centred phenotype across the few reported patients, including a JIA-like presentation in later cases.

steps/3.description: The characteristic clinical expression of MPS IX is periarticular soft-tissue masses with episodic painful joint swelling, together with mild short stature and acetabular erosions. Neurological and visceral involvement are absent. Some later-reported patients are clinically indistinguishable from juvenile idiopathic arthritis, with proliferative synovitis.

evidence.snippet: This patient had a surprisingly mild clinical phenotype, including notable periarticular soft tissue masses, mild short stature, an absence of neurological or visceral involvement, and histological and ultrastructural evidence of a lysosomal storage disease.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents periarticular soft-tissue masses as a defining MPS IX feature.

evidence.snippet: The first reported patient had mild short stature and periarticular soft tissue masses; the other reported patients are clinically indistinguishable from juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms periarticular soft-tissue masses in the index MPS IX patient.

steps/4.description: Notable periarticular soft-tissue masses, accompanied by episodes of painful joint swelling, are the hallmark feature of MPS IX. No precise HPO term exists for periarticular soft-tissue masses, so this is annotated to the closest available term, Joint swelling.

evidence.snippet: This patient had a surprisingly mild clinical phenotype, including notable periarticular soft tissue masses, mild short stature, an absence of neurological or visceral involvement, and histological and ultrastructural evidence of a lysosomal storage disease.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents mild short stature as a core MPS IX feature.

evidence.snippet: The first reported patient had mild short stature and periarticular soft tissue masses; the other reported patients are clinically indistinguishable from juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms mild short stature in the first reported MPS IX patient.

steps/5.description: Mild short stature is part of the MPS IX phenotype and is notably milder than the disproportionate short stature of the sulfated-GAG mucopolysaccharidoses.

evidence.snippet: The first reported patient had mild short stature and periarticular soft tissue masses; the other reported patients are clinically indistinguishable from juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
evidence.explanation: The JIA-indistinguishable presentation of later patients supports inflammatory joint swelling as part of the MPS IX phenotype.

steps/6.description: Episodic painful joint swelling occurs in MPS IX, sometimes mimicking juvenile idiopathic arthritis with proliferative synovitis.

evidence.snippet: This patient had a surprisingly mild clinical phenotype, including notable periarticular soft tissue masses, mild short stature, an absence of neurological or visceral involvement, and histological and ultrastructural evidence of a lysosomal storage disease.
evidence.explanation: Histological and ultrastructural evidence of lysosomal storage in the hyaluronidase-deficient patient supports lysosomal accumulation of the undegraded substrate.

edges/1.description: Loss of hyaluronidase 1 activity leaves hyaluronan undegraded, so it accumulates within lysosomes.

evidence.snippet: This patient had a surprisingly mild clinical phenotype, including notable periarticular soft tissue masses, mild short stature, an absence of neurological or visceral involvement, and histological and ultrastructural evidence of a lysosomal storage disease.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the hyaluronidase-deficiency storage state to periarticular soft-tissue masses and the broader mild joint-centred phenotype.

edges/2.description: Hyaluronan storage in and around joints produces periarticular soft-tissue masses and joint disease.

edges/3.description: Hyaluronan storage produces periarticular soft-tissue masses.

edges/4.description: Joint-centered hyaluronan storage manifests as episodic painful joint swelling.

edges/5.description: The joint-centered lysosomal storage phenotype includes mild short stature.

evidence.snippet: We further show that these two hyaluronidase genes, as well as a third recently discovered adjacent hyaluronidase gene, HYAL3, have markedly different tissue expression patterns, consistent with differing roles in HA metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Documents HYAL1 within the tandem HYAL1/HYAL2/HYAL3 cluster and the distinct tissue expression that underlies the restricted MPS IX phenotype.

treatments/0.description: There is no approved enzyme replacement therapy or other disease-modifying treatment for MPS IX. Management is supportive and symptomatic, directed at joint pain, swelling, and the periarticular soft-tissue masses (e.g. analgesia/anti-inflammatory measures and orthopaedic/symptomatic care).

evidence.snippet: Arylsulfatase K (ARSK) is a recently characterised lysosomal hydrolase involved in GAG degradation that removes the 2-O-sulfate group from 2-sulfoglucuronate.
evidence.explanation: Defines the enzymatic step that is lost in MPS X: lysosomal removal of the 2-O-sulfate from 2-sulfoglucuronate during glycosaminoglycan degradation.

evidence.snippet: Human HT1080 cells expressing the ARSK-Leu187Ter construct exhibited absent protein levels by western blot, and cells with the ARSK-Arg84Cys construct showed markedly reduced enzyme activity in an ARSK-specific enzymatic assay against 2-O-sulfoglucuronate-containing disaccharides as analysed by C18-reversed-phase chromatography followed by MS.
evidence.explanation: Functional proof that the two founding variants cause loss of ARSK activity, by absent protein and by loss of catalytic activity respectively.

evidence.snippet: The arginine at amino acid position 84 in ARSK is part of the highly conserved sulfatase signature 80-CCPSR-84
evidence.explanation: Locates the p.Arg84Cys missense lesion in the sulfatase signature motif, explaining why a stably expressed protein is catalytically inactive.

evidence.snippet: ARSK-S356Y completely abolished the ARSK enzyme activity compared with the wild-type (ARSK-WT)
evidence.explanation: A second, independently identified missense allele is also catalytically null, supporting loss of enzyme activity as the shared molecular lesion.

steps/1.description:
Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ARSK abolish or severely reduce the activity of arylsulfatase K, the lysosomal sulfatase that removes the 2-O-sulfate group from 2-sulfoglucuronate. Reported variants act through two distinct routes to the same end point. Nonsense alleles (p.Leu187Ter, p.Tyr417Ter) yield no detectable protein, consistent with nonsense-mediated decay. Missense alleles are catalytically dead while remaining stably expressed: p.Arg84Cys disrupts the conserved sulfatase signature 80-CCPSR-84 that is required to convert the active-site cysteine to formylglycine, and p.Ser356Tyr abolishes activity within the sulfatase domain without destabilizing the protein. Because sulfatases show high substrate specificity and no functional redundancy, no other human sulfatase compensates for the lost step.
Term-binding note: the molecular function below is bound to GO:0008484 (sulfuric ester hydrolase activity), a broad parent, deliberately. GO has no term for glucuronate 2-O-sulfatase (glucuronate 2-sulfatase, GDS) activity, and no sibling sulfatase term fits - ARSK is specific for the 2-O-sulfate of 2-sulfoglucuronate and does not share substrates with the other lysosomal sulfatases. Binding a narrower but wrong term would misstate the enzymology, so the accurate parent is preferred over a manufactured match. A GO term request for the specific activity is the way to improve this.

evidence.snippet: Glucuronate-2-O-sulfation occurs in HS, DS and CS and, during degradation, is selectively removed by ARSK
evidence.explanation: Establishes which GAG species carry the ARSK-dependent modification, and hence which are stalled when the enzyme is lost.

evidence.snippet: Mild elevation of dermatan sulfate was detected in the two subjects investigated by LC-MS/MS.
evidence.explanation: Dermatan sulfate is the GAG species measurably elevated in patients, supporting the restricted, dermatan-biased character of the storage.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical analyses reveal variable dermatan sulfate (DS) excretion in urine, with some patients showing increased DS, while others had normal urinary glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), suggesting that a normal GAG profile does not exclude this condition.
evidence.explanation: Identifies dermatan sulfate as the affected species. Marked INDIRECT because the quote reports urinary excretion, from which lysosomal storage follows only by inference, and because it simultaneously establishes that the signal is inconsistent and can be undetectable by routine assays - the qualification this node depends on.

steps/2.description: Partially degraded heparan sulfate, dermatan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate fragments terminating in 2-O-sulfoglucuronate accumulate in lysosomes. This is the GAG-accumulation hub of the mps_gag_storage module, but the storage burden is far smaller than in the other mucopolysaccharidoses and is engaged in a highly restricted way. Glucuronate-2-O-sulfation is an uncommon modification rather than a backbone-defining one, so only the minority of chains carrying it are blocked; the bulk of heparan, dermatan, and chondroitin sulfate is still catabolized normally. The module's heparan-sulfate neuronopathic arm and its keratan-sulfate skeletal arm are therefore not engaged - keratan sulfate is not an ARSK substrate, and no reported patient has CNS disease. Only the dermatan-sulfate connective-tissue arm is engaged, and even that partially: dermatan sulfate is the one GAG species reproducibly elevated in patient urine, and the downstream disease is confined to chondro-osseous and cardiac connective tissue rather than the generalized visceral storage of MPS I or VI.

evidence.snippet: Remarkably, all patients showed metaphyseal striation of the long bones, a crucial diagnostic clue to identify ARSK-related MPS type 10.
evidence.explanation: Identifies metaphyseal striation as the consistent radiographic marker of the chondro-osseous arm across an independent patient series.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, vertebral involvement regressed during follow-up. On the other hand, hip dysplasia progressed in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports the divergent natural history annotated here: regressing vertebral disease with progressive hip disease.

evidence.snippet: While typical dysostosis multiplex findings were not observed, mild platyspondyly with anterior beaking of some vertebral bodies, irregular vertebral endplates, wide ribs, inferior tapering of the ilea with a poorly developed acetabulum, irregularity of the central part of the femoral head, delayed ossification of the carpals were noted.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the skeletal findings and states explicitly that classic dysostosis multiplex is absent, which is the discriminating feature of this node relative to the other mucopolysaccharidoses.

steps/3.description: The dominant and near-universal disease arm of MPS X. Cartilage and bone-forming tissue develop an epiphyseal, metaphyseal, and vertebral dysplasia that presents clinically as hip and knee pain with a waddling gait in mid-childhood, and radiographically as metaphyseal striation of the long bones, platyspondyly with anterior vertebral beaking, delayed carpal ossification, small epiphyses, and inferior tapering of the ilia with a poorly formed acetabulum. Two features of its natural history distinguish it from the other mucopolysaccharidoses: the vertebral changes regress with time rather than progressing, while the hip dysplasia progresses in every reported patient, so the hip rather than the spine is the long-term burden. The picture is close enough to spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, and bilateral Legg-Calve-Perthes disease that every published patient carried one of those labels before sequencing.

evidence.snippet: Heart abnormalities in S1 and S2 included cardiac murmur (aortic or mitral), valve disease, thickened leaflets and regurgitation.
evidence.explanation: Documents the valvular connective-tissue involvement that defines this node.

evidence.snippet: Mild aortic valve stenosis and mild left ventricular hypertrophy were noted in cardiac ultrasound in S1 and S2.
evidence.explanation: Documents the stenotic and ventricular findings of this node on echocardiography.

steps/4.description: A mild and late arm of the disease, found only on deliberate targeted assessment after the genetic diagnosis is made. Reported findings are an aortic or mitral murmur, valve thickening with regurgitation, mild aortic valve stenosis, and mild left ventricular hypertrophy suggesting early storage cardiomyopathy. Curated separately from the ocular arm below because the two have different evidence: the later series that found normal eye examinations throughout did not report absent cardiac involvement, so a single bundled node would leave it ambiguous which half its refuting evidence applied to.

evidence.snippet: reverse phenotyping revealed mild opacity of the lens and vitreous body
evidence.explanation: Documents the ocular finding in the index family.

evidence.snippet: All patients showed normal intelligence, normal hearing and eye examinations, and none had organomegaly.
evidence.explanation: Cuts directly against this node: an independent series found normal eye examinations in every patient. Now that the ocular arm is its own node, this REFUTE is unambiguous about what it refutes.

steps/5.description: The most variable arm of the disease, and the one with directly conflicting evidence. The index family showed mild lens and vitreous opacity, with loss of the retinal interdigitation zone temporal to the macula on optical coherence tomography in one patient. Two independent later series reported normal eye examinations throughout. This arm is therefore genuinely inconsistent between kindreds rather than merely under-ascertained, which is why it is recorded with both supporting and refuting evidence rather than being asserted or dropped. It remains the basis for offering ophthalmological surveillance once MPS X is diagnosed.

evidence.snippet: The patients' initial complaints were hip or knee pain and a waddling gait.
evidence.explanation: Establishes joint pain as the presenting symptom of MPS X.

steps/6.description: Hip, knee, thigh, leg, and back pain is the usual presenting complaint, typically beginning between 7 and 11 years of age and severe enough to limit walking distance in some patients.

evidence.snippet: The patients' initial complaints were hip or knee pain and a waddling gait.
evidence.explanation: Establishes waddling gait as a presenting feature.

steps/7.description: A waddling gait, reflecting hip disease, is present from toddlerhood in some patients and is one of the two features that most consistently bring affected children to medical attention.

evidence.snippet: The affected individuals usually present with progressive hip joint abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Review of all reported patients establishes progressive hip involvement as the usual presentation.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, vertebral involvement regressed during follow-up. On the other hand, hip dysplasia progressed in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the progressive clinical course annotated here.

steps/8.description: Progressive hip dysplasia with acetabular hypoplasia and inferior tapering of the ilia. Unlike the vertebral changes, hip disease worsened over follow-up in every patient in whom it was tracked, making it the principal long-term morbidity of MPS X.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral LCPD should result in considering the possibility of MPS type X as well as other MPS subtypes
evidence.explanation: Establishes bilateral Legg-Calve-Perthes disease as an MPS X presentation and a diagnostic prompt.

steps/9.description: Femoral head osteonecrosis, generally bilateral, radiographically indistinguishable from Legg-Calve-Perthes disease. Several reported patients carried a bilateral Legg-Calve-Perthes diagnosis for years before ARSK sequencing; bilateral disease is the clue that should prompt consideration of a mucopolysaccharidosis.

evidence.snippet: Remarkably, all patients showed metaphyseal striation of the long bones, a crucial diagnostic clue to identify ARSK-related MPS type 10.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the near-universal frequency and the diagnostic value.

steps/10.description: Vertical striation of the metaphyses of the long bones, particularly the distal femur and tibia. This is the single most consistent radiographic finding in MPS X and is present at younger ages than the vertebral or facial changes.

evidence.snippet: The main radiological abnormalities in all four subjects were thickened calvaria, platyspondyly, anterior inferior beaking of the thoracolumbar vertebrae, broadening of clavicles and ribs, narrowing of lower parts of iliac bones, small epiphyses, metaphysial striae, and hypoplastic carpal bones
evidence.explanation: Documents platyspondyly with anterior beaking in all four index patients.

steps/11.description: Flattened, broad vertebral bodies with anterior inferior beaking of the thoracolumbar spine, irregular endplates, and posterior endplate scalloping. Notably, vertebral involvement regressed on follow-up in one series rather than progressing.

evidence.snippet: Radiological changes were not present in the hand of Individual 1 at age 2 years, but at age 8 years 5 months several carpal bones were either not ossified or small for his age.
evidence.explanation: Documents defective carpal ossification and its emergence during childhood rather than at birth.

steps/12.description: Carpal bones unossified or small for age, with retarded bone age. This is an early finding: one sibling had a normal wrist radiograph at age 2 years and defective carpal ossification by age 9.

evidence.snippet: coarse facial features, short trunk disproportionate short stature and short neck, genua valga, and hip pain were noticed at the end of the first decade
evidence.explanation: Documents short-trunk disproportionate short stature and its end-of-first-decade onset.

steps/13.description: Short-trunk disproportionate short stature with a short neck and relative macrocephaly, noticed at the end of the first decade. As with coarse facies, this is age dependent and absent in younger children.

evidence.snippet: Heart abnormalities in S1 and S2 included cardiac murmur (aortic or mitral), valve disease, thickened leaflets and regurgitation.
evidence.explanation: Documents valve thickening and regurgitation.

steps/14.description: Valve leaflet thickening with regurgitation and an aortic or mitral murmur, found on targeted echocardiography after molecular diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Mild aortic valve stenosis and mild left ventricular hypertrophy were noted in cardiac ultrasound in S1 and S2.
evidence.explanation: Documents mild aortic stenosis and ventricular hypertrophy.

steps/15.description: Mild aortic valve stenosis with mild left ventricular hypertrophy suggesting early storage cardiomyopathy.

evidence.snippet: reverse phenotyping revealed mild opacity of the lens and vitreous body
evidence.explanation: Documents the lens and vitreous opacity.

steps/16.description: Mild lens and vitreous opacity, with loss of the retinal interdigitation zone temporal to the macula on optical coherence tomography in one patient. Absent in two later series, so this is a variable rather than defining feature.

evidence.snippet: Arsk-deficient mice show, in an organ-specific manner, a moderate accumulation of HS and CS metabolites characterized by 2-O-sulfated glucuronate moieties at their non-reducing ends.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates that loss of ARSK causes accumulation of GAG metabolites capped by the very modification ARSK removes, establishing the causal link from enzyme loss to substrate storage.

edges/1.description: With the 2-O-desulfation step blocked, exolytic degradation stalls at every chain terminus bearing a 2-O-sulfated glucuronate, and the partially degraded fragments accumulate in the lysosome.

evidence.snippet: The main radiological abnormalities in all four subjects were thickened calvaria, platyspondyly, anterior inferior beaking of the thoracolumbar vertebrae, broadening of clavicles and ribs, narrowing of lower parts of iliac bones, small epiphyses, metaphysial striae, and hypoplastic carpal bones
evidence.explanation: Documents the chondro-osseous consequence of ARSK deficiency as a consistent epiphyseal, metaphyseal, and vertebral dysplasia.

edges/2.description: Storage in cartilage and bone-forming tissue disturbs epiphyseal and metaphyseal development, producing the skeletal disease that dominates MPS X. The intermediate steps between fragment accumulation and disturbed endochondral ossification have not been worked out in this disorder, so the link is annotated as indirect.

evidence.snippet: Reverse phenotyping in two of the four individuals revealed additional cardiac and ophthalmological abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that cardiac and ocular involvement occurs, and that it is subclinical enough to require deliberate targeted assessment.

edges/3.description: Dermatan-sulfate-biased storage in valvular connective tissue produces the mild, late cardiac findings of MPS X.

evidence.snippet: Reverse phenotyping in two of the four individuals revealed additional cardiac and ophthalmological abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that ophthalmological involvement occurs and is subclinical enough to require deliberate targeted assessment.

edges/4.description: Dermatan-sulfate-biased storage in ocular connective tissue produces the lens and vitreous opacity reported in the index family.

edges/5.description: Progressive acetabular and femoral head dysplasia is the dominant skeletal burden.

edges/6.description: Femoral head involvement presents as a Legg-Calve-Perthes-like osteonecrosis, usually bilateral.

edges/7.description: Vertical metaphyseal striation of the long bones is the consistent radiographic marker.

edges/8.description: Vertebral body flattening with anterior beaking and irregular endplates.

edges/9.description: Hip, knee, and back pain is the usual presenting complaint.

edges/10.description: Hip disease produces the waddling gait that typically brings the child to attention.

edges/11.description: Carpal bones are unossified or small for age.

edges/12.description: Vertebral involvement produces short-trunk disproportion, but only in older patients; younger children are of normal stature and proportion.

edges/13.description: Valve leaflet thickening with regurgitation.

edges/14.description: Mild aortic valve stenosis on echocardiography.

edges/15.description: Mild lens and vitreous opacity found on slit-lamp examination.

evidence.snippet: Both children were homozygous, and both parents heterozygous, for a predicted stop variant in ARSK
evidence.explanation: Documents the nonsense allele and its segregation.

evidence.snippet: we identified a novel homozygous missense germline variant, c.1067C>A (p.S356Y), in the ARSK gene
evidence.explanation: Documents the p.Ser356Tyr missense allele.

evidence.snippet: In gnomAD, this variant is listed with a total allele frequency of 0.002129% (6/281810 alleles).
evidence.explanation: Documents the population rarity of the founding allele, supporting the rarity annotated in features.

evidence.snippet: It will be very important to develop enzyme replacement therapy and potentially other treatments, given the pain and disability associated with this disorder.
